content: 1. Cisplatin, colistin, polymyxin B, vancomycin, and viomycin should be used cautiously due to their potential for ototoxicity. Avoid using potent diuretics such as ethacrynic acid or furosemide, as they can increase the risk of ototoxicity. When administered intravenously, diuretics may enhance aminoglycoside toxicity by altering antibiotic concentrations in serum and tissues. 2. Patients with a history of aminoglycoside toxicity or hypersensitivity should be closely monitored when treated with aminoglycosides, as these drugs carry a high risk of toxicity. Signs of ototoxicity, such as tinnitus or vertigo, may indicate vestibular injury and impending bilateral irreversible damage. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if ototoxicity is suspected. 3. Aminoglycosides also carry a risk of nephrotoxicity. Factors that increase the risk of ototoxicity include advanced age and dehydration. These drugs have a narrow therapeutic index and are not intended for long-term therapy. 4. Use aminoglycosides with caution in patients with renal failure (not on dialysis), myasthenia gravis, hypocalcemia, or conditions that depress neuromuscular transmission. Dosage adjustments are necessary in cases of renal impairment. 5. For endocarditis prophylaxis during gastrointestinal (GI) or genitourinary (GU) procedures, the American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines recommend aminoglycosides only for high-risk patients. 6. Diuretics may enhance aminoglycoside toxicity by altering antibiotic concentrations in serum and tissues. Certain diuretics, such as ethacrynic acid or furosemide, may independently cause ototoxicity. Potent diuretics should be avoided. 7. Exercise caution in patients with electrolyte abnormalities, including hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, or hypokalemia. Similarly, caution is advised in patients with neuromuscular disorders, such as myasthenia gravis, or those with hearing and renal impairments. 8. Aminoglycosides are classified as Pregnancy Category D. They enter breast milk, so caution is advised during lactation. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) states that aminoglycosides are compatible with nursing. 9. The volume of distribution (Vd) of aminoglycosides is approximately 0.3 L/kg. This value increases in conditions such as edema, ascites, and fluid overload, and decreases in dehydration. The half-life of aminoglycosides is 2–3 hours in patients with normal renal function (NRF). Renal clearance is directly related to renal function, with 70% of the drug excreted unchanged in the urine in patients with NRF. 10. Aminoglycosides may have additive effects with other drugs, such as amphotericin B, ampicillin, cefazolin, dopamine, furosemide, and heparin. Compatibility varies depending on the method of administration (e.g., syringe, Y-site). For example, ampicillin and heparin are compatible in syringes, while furosemide and heparin are compatible at Y-sites. 11. For intravenous administration, dilute a single dose of aminoglycosides in 50–200 mL of normal saline (NS) or 5% dextrose in water (D5W). Infuse the solution over 30 minutes to 2 hours. After infusion, flush the line with NS or D5W. 12. Topical gentamicin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat bacterial skin infections, such as impetigo or folliculitis. It is also used for infections associated with skin conditions like eczema or psoriasis, as well as infected burns, sores, or wounds. However, its appropriateness depends on the specific bacteria causing the infection, as resistance may reduce its effectiveness. 13. Topical gentamicin works by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, effectively killing certain types of bacteria. 14. Topical gentamicin is available as a 1% cream or ointment for application to the skin. It should be stored at room temperature (68–77°F or 20–25°C) but can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59–86°F (15–30°C). 15. Common side effects of topical gentamicin include skin redness, itching, and irritation. If these side effects are bothersome, patients should inform their healthcare provider. Serious side effects, such as severe allergic reactions, require immediate medical attention. Symptoms of an allergic reaction include breathing difficulties, wheezing, rapid heartbeat, fever, swollen lymph nodes, facial swelling, throat tightness, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, stomach cramps, or joint pain. 16. Topical gentamicin may lead to secondary infections caused by other organisms, such as fungi. 17. Patients allergic to gentamicin or any ingredients in the product should not use topical gentamicin. Pharmacists can provide a complete list of ingredients in specific products. 18. Topical gentamicin should only be used as prescribed by a healthcare provider. It is for external use only and should not be applied to the eyes. For impetigo treatment, crusts should be removed before application to allow the antibiotic to reach the infection. 19. Before using topical gentamicin, patients should inform their healthcare provider about all health conditions, medications, and supplements they are taking. This information helps determine if the medication is appropriate. 20. The effects of topical gentamicin on pregnancy and breastfeeding are not well understood. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals should consult their healthcare provider before use. 21. There are no known interactions between topical gentamicin and foods, drinks, or other medications. However, patients should complete the full course of treatment to prevent antibiotic resistance. 22. In case of an overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or contacting a poison control center at 800-222-1222. 23. If a dose is missed, apply it as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with the regular schedule. Do not double doses. Completing the prescribed course is essential to reduce the risk of resistance.
